title: Having a Coaching Framework Isn't Enough. Here's What the Data Actually Requires.
summary: 77% of revenue organizations have some form of coaching framework. Only 38% execute it consistently. New benchmark data reveals the performance gap that inconsistency creates — and what closing it actually takes.
body_markdown:
There's a version of the sales coaching conversation that most organizations have had and feel good about. It looks something like this:


They've adopted a framework. Maybe MEDDIC, GROW, Sandler—something structured that gives managers a consistent approach to coaching conversations. They've run trainings against the framework. They've documented the processes that need to be followed. Somewhere in a shared drive, the coaching playbook exists.


And then the quarter happens, and the numbers look about the same as before.


New data from Ambition's State of Sales Coaching in 2026 helps explain why — and the answer isn't that the framework is wrong.


[Download The State of Sales Coaching in 2026 here.](https://ambition.com/resources/the-state-of-sales-coaching-in-2026)


### The Adoption Gap


When we asked over 300 revenue leaders whether their organization has a standardized coaching framework, 77% said yes.


However, when we asked whether that framework is consistently adopted across all of their managers, only 38% said yes.


The gap between those two numbers—77% with *a* framework and 38% with a framework that's *consistently used* —is where most organizations' coaching ROI disappears.


Here's what that gap looks like in terms of quota attainment:


- Consistent framework, consistently adopted: 37% of organizations report 71%+ quota attainment
- Framework exists, adoption varies by manager: 28% report 71%+ quota attainment
- No framework — coaching left to individual managers: 22% report 71%+ quota attainment


Notice what's happening there. The jump from no framework to an inconsistently adopted framework is meaningful at 6 points. But the jump from inconsistent adoption to consistent adoption is bigger: 9 points. And the difference between "we have a framework" and "our managers all execute it" is the largest performance gap in the survey data.


A coaching playbook nobody follows is ultimately just a document.


### The Quality Problem That Makes It Worse


Inconsistent framework adoption isn't the only consistency problem in the data. Coaching quality tells a similar story.


When we asked revenue leaders to describe coaching quality across their manager team, we found:


- 35% describe coaching quality as "highly variable" (quality depends heavily on the individual manager)
- 12% say they have no way to measure coaching quality at all
- Only 26% report very consistent quality across their team


That last number is the one that should get your attention. In a well-functioning coaching operation, every rep should have roughly the same experience of being coached, regardless of which manager they report to. In reality, only about 1 in 4 organizations are achieving that.


And the performance implications are significant: organizations with very consistent coaching quality across their manager team achieve 71%+ quota attainment at a rate 54% higher than those with highly variable quality (40% vs. 26%).


The jump from "somewhat consistent" to "very consistent" quality (aka from good to great) is larger than any coaching frequency improvement in our dataset. More consistent quality is worth more than more frequent coaching.


### You Can't Improve What You Can't See


Here's the underlying problem that connects inconsistent framework adoption and variable coaching quality: most organizations don't have visibility into either.


When 47% of your revenue leaders describe coaching quality as either highly variable or completely unmeasurable, they're describing an organization flying blind on one of its most important performance levers. The managers who coach exceptionally well are doing it through skill, instinct, or both — but their approach isn't being replicated. The managers who are struggling aren't being identified and supported. And the leaders above them have no way to know which situation they're in.


This is the difference between a coaching strategy and a coaching system. A strategy tells you what good coaching looks like. A system gives you the visibility and structure to ensure it's actually happening — consistently, across every manager, every week.


### What Consistent Looks Like in Practice


The organizations that have cracked this aren't doing anything exotic. But they share a few things:


**Frameworks are operationalized, not just documented.** Rather than training managers on a coaching methodology and hoping they use it, these organizations build the framework into the coaching process itself. That includes pre-meeting templates that surface the right questions, session structures that follow the methodology, and post-coaching notes that create accountability.


**Quality is measured, not assumed.** Whether through conversation intelligence, manager observation, or rep feedback loops, high-performing organizations have some mechanism for knowing whether coaching sessions are actually productive. What gets measured can be improved; what doesn't gets averaged out.


**Manager-to-manager variance is treated as a system problem, not a talent problem.** When one manager runs exceptional coaching sessions and another runs check-ins that never go deeper than pipeline review, the instinct is to coach the weaker manager. The more durable solution is to reduce how much the session depends on the individual manager's approach through structure, tooling, and accountability.


### The Benchmark Is Useful. The Gap Is Actionable.


One of the clearest things our survey data shows is that the coaching consistency gap between organizations that have a framework and organizations where that framework is actually executed is not negligible. It's a 15-point difference in the share of organizations hitting strong quota attainment.


That gap only closes when the system around the playbook ensures consistent execution.
